Helping your child through a stressful week

Updated: November 17, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

On Tuesday your child needs to finish a project, pack for swimming and find something for a class presentation. By dinner a small question brings tears. Before trying a calming exercise, ask which part feels like too much. Maybe the first useful step is taking one thing off the list.

Find the pressure you can change

Ask about a particular moment: “Was it harder to start the project, or to think about showing it to the class?” Listen without insisting they look on the bright side. Notice sleep, meals and time for play. If the week has become too crowded, agree what can be simplified or postponed. If the child mentions bullying, a threat or an unsafe activity, address that problem with the responsible adult.

Separate what has to happen from what would merely be nice. A school project might need three clear ideas and a title, even if the child wants a perfect drawing on every page. Ask what the teacher actually requested. Name something concrete that already works, such as explaining the first idea in their own words.

Offer company before offering a solution

Some children want you to sit near them. Others want a quiet break, a short walk or to talk as you wash dishes. Ask instead of assuming. When you are under pressure yourself, describe one manageable response aloud: “I’ve got two things due. I’m going to write them down and ask which one can wait.”

In a laboratory study, 61 girls aged seven to twelve did a stressful speaking and arithmetic task. Afterward they were assigned to contact with their mother in person, by phone or to a period without contact. By the end, stress-hormone levels in the two contact groups were similar and near their starting levels. This short experiment measured cortisol in one group of children. It does not establish a special phrase, a required caregiver or how fast every child should settle.

Prepare for one unfamiliar moment

If the class presentation is the sticking point, let the child choose a small rehearsal. They might say the first sentence to you, or ask the teacher where they will stand. Recognise the specific effort it took, even if they still felt nervous. Avoid forcing a child into something unsafe or promising that fear must disappear in a set time.

Make room for a familiar enjoyable activity and check back afterward: “Did the shorter list help? What is still hard?” Contact the child's clinician if distress persists, repeatedly interferes with sleep, eating, school or play, or there are recurring physical symptoms. Get urgent help if a child speaks about harming themselves. If they may act soon or you cannot keep them safe, stay with them and seek emergency help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask which demand feels hardest before offering advice.

Change one practical thing and tell the child how you handled your own pressure.

Seek assessment for persistent distress, disruption or repeated physical symptoms.

How BeMama can help

BeMama suggests letting your child cross one optional task off the family's list and choose when you will check whether the change made the day easier.

When to seek help

Seek urgent professional help for talk of self-harm. If a child may hurt themselves imminently or you cannot keep them safe, stay with them and call emergency services. A clinician can help with persistent distress or changes in sleep, eating or participation.

Evidence notes updated: November 17, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Find one demand that can change and agree who will change it.
  • Offer support the child wants and notice effort without requiring perfection.
  • Check whether a change helped and seek advice if distress keeps disrupting daily life.

Frequently asked questions

What can help a child feel less stressed today?

Listen for the hardest moment, then choose one small change such as clearing space for a break or asking a teacher to clarify a deadline. The child can name something that went well without having to pretend everything is fine.

How can a parent reduce pressure?

Review what you are expecting of them this week. A task can be good enough without being perfect. Protect time for food, sleep and something enjoyable as well as the work that needs doing.

How can we prepare for a new situation?

Explain what will happen, invite questions and let the child practise a small safe part first. Acknowledge their effort and ask what they want to try next.

How can I teach stress management?

Let your child see you pause, ask for help or change a plan. When they are calm, practise one approach together and ask later whether it helped. Different situations may need different responses.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
